sentences.text: Atsinganosaurus was a slender titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur that lived in what is now France during the Late Cretaceous.
Its teeth featured cylindrical roots and spatulate crowns, adaptations suited for processing tough vegetation.
The animal's sacrum, a series of fused vertebrae connecting the spine to the pelvis, consisted of five bones with a concave posterior surface, a condition known as opisthocoelous.
Additionally, the distal end of the humerus, or upper arm bone, expanded in a slightly oblique manner.
Atsinganosaurus holds the distinction of being the fourth Late Cretaceous European titanosaurian discovered, following Lirainosaurus, Ampelosaurus, and Magyarosaurus.
Remarkably, the well-preserved bones of this species were found confined to an area of just six square meters.
The fossil site of La Bastide Neuve near Velaux in the Bouches-du-Rhône department was first discovered in 1992 by Xavier Valentin.
Excavations at the Velaux-La Bastide Neuve site were subsequently carried out between 2009 and 2010 by the Palaios Association and the University of Poitiers.
Atsinganosaurus was first described by Géraldine Garcia, Sauveur Amico, Francois Fournier, Eudes Thouand, and Xavier Valentin in 2010.

The only known remains were collected from the Grès à Reptiles Formation of the Aix-en-Provence Basin, where the holotype consists of four posterior dorsal vertebrae discovered alongside remains of another titanosaurian named Garrigatitan.
Fossils of Atsinganosaurus were found alongside remains of turtles, crocodilian teeth, theropods, nodosaurids, and rhadinodontids.
Later estimates suggest adults of Atsinganosaurus reached lengths of 5.38 to 8.95 meters and weighed between 2.46 and 5.26 metric tons.
A 2018 cladistic analysis places Atsinganosaurus in the lithostrotian clade Lirainosaurinae alongside Ampelosaurus and Lirainosaurus.

It is suggested that Atsinganosaurus is a basal representative of Lithostrotia based on a combination of primitive and derived titanosaurian features, though no published phylogenetic analysis confirms this.
Atsinganosaurus lived approximately 75 million years ago during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now Europe.
The time range for Atsinganosaurus is estimated to be between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
The generic name Atsinganosaurus derives from the Greek word for "gypsy," referring to a possible east-to-west migration of the species.
